name: Introduce the formal notation used for MLP training (sets of neurons, potentials, outputs, weights, \(j_{\leftarrow}\) and \(j_{\rightarrow}\), the formal unit input) and define the activity of an MLP in this notation.
answer:
Architecture (recap): neurons are partitioned into layers numbered from 0 (input layer); neurons of the \(i\)-th layer are connected with all neurons of the \((i+1)\)-st layer.

Notation:
• \(X\) – the set of input neurons, \(Y\) – the set of output neurons, \(Z\) – the set of all neurons (\(X,Y\subseteq Z\));
• individual neurons are denoted by indices \(i,j\), etc.;
• \(\xi_j\) – the inner potential of neuron \(j\) after the computation stops;
• \(y_j\) – the output of neuron \(j\) after the computation stops; the formal unit input is denoted by index \(0\notin Z\) and has \(y_0=1\);
• \(w_{ji}\) – the weight of the connection from \(i\) to \(j\) (in particular \(w_{j0}=b_j\) is the weight from the formal unit input, i.e. the bias of neuron \(j\));
• \(j_{\leftarrow}\) – the set of all \(i\) such that there is an arc to \(j\) from \(i\); we also put \(0\in j_{\leftarrow}\) for every \(j\in Z\setminus X\) (so the bias is included in the sums below);
• \(j_{\rightarrow}\) – the set of all \(i\) such that there is an arc from \(j\) to \(i\).

Activity:
• inner potential of neuron \(j\): \(\displaystyle\xi_j=\sum_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}w_{ji}y_i\);
• each neuron \(j\) has an activation function \(\sigma_j\) (arbitrary differentiable);
• the state of a non-input neuron \(j\in Z\setminus X\) after the computation stops: \(y_j=\sigma_j(\xi_j)\). Since \(y_j\) depends on the configuration \(w\) and the input \(x\), we sometimes write \(y_j(w,x)\);
• the network computes a function from \(\mathbb R^{\lvert X\rvert}\) to \(\mathbb R^{\lvert Y\rvert}\). Layer-wise computation: first, all input neurons are assigned the values of the input; in the \(\ell\)-th step, all neurons of the \(\ell\)-th layer are evaluated.
keyPoints: \(w_{ji}\) = weight of the connection from \(i\) to \(j\); \(w_{j0}=b_j\) belongs to the formal unit input \(y_0=1\), \(0\in j_{\leftarrow}\)
Network computes \(\mathbb R^{\lvert X\rvert}\to\mathbb R^{\lvert Y\rvert}\) layer by layer
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 83–84 (the slides write w_{j0}=b_j; the older deck had w_{j0}=-b_j)

name: Define the training dataset and the (squared) error function of an MLP, and describe the batch gradient descent algorithm. State the normalisation convention of the error function.
answer:
Training dataset: \(T=\{(x_k,d_k)\mid k=1,\dots,p\}\), where every \(x_k\in\mathbb R^{\lvert X\rvert}\) is an input vector and every \(d_k\in\mathbb R^{\lvert Y\rvert}\) is the desired network output. For \(j\in Y\), \(d_{kj}\) denotes the desired output of neuron \(j\) for the network input \(x_k\), so \(d_k=(d_{kj})_{j\in Y}\).

Error function (convention of this course: the average over the training set): \[ E(w)=\frac1p\sum_{k=1}^{p}E_k(w),\qquad E_k(w)=\frac12\sum_{j\in Y}\bigl(y_j(w,x_k)-d_{kj}\bigr)^2. \] This is just an example of an error function; other error functions come later. If \(E\) is defined as a plain sum without \(1/p\), all gradients are \(p\) times larger, which is equivalent to rescaling the learning rate \(\varepsilon\) by \(p\) – only the scale of \(\varepsilon\) changes.

Batch algorithm (gradient descent): it computes a sequence of weight vectors \(w^{(0)},w^{(1)},w^{(2)},\dots\)
• the weights in \(w^{(0)}\) are randomly initialized to values close to 0;
• in step \(t+1\) (\(t=0,1,2,\dots\)): \[ w_{ji}^{(t+1)}=w_{ji}^{(t)}+\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)},\qquad \Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}=-\varepsilon(t)\cdot\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr), \] where \(0\lt\varepsilon(t)\le1\) is the learning rate in step \(t+1\).

Since \(\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}(w^{(t)})\) is a component of the gradient \(\nabla E\), the update has the vector form \(w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}-\varepsilon(t)\,\nabla E(w^{(t)})\). The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase of \(E\), so the algorithm moves the weights against it. It is called batch because every step uses the error over the whole training set.
keyPoints: A plain sum instead of the average only rescales \(\varepsilon\) by \(p\)
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 85–86

name: Derive the formula for the partial derivative of one example's error \(E_k\) with respect to a weight \(w_{ji}\) of an MLP with the chain rule, and state how the gradient of the whole error \(E\) is obtained from it.
answer:
Setting. \(E=\frac1p\sum_{k=1}^{p}E_k\), potentials \(\xi_j=\sum_{r\in j_{\leftarrow}}w_{jr}y_r\), outputs \(y_j=\sigma_j(\xi_j)\). All values \(y_j\) are in fact \(y_j(w,x_k)\). Here \(\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}\) denotes the derivative of \(E_k\) viewed as a function of the outputs of the neurons in the layer of \(j\): for fixed \(w\) and \(x_k\) these outputs determine the values of all neurons in the layers above, and hence also \(E_k\).

Whole error. By linearity of differentiation, for every weight \(w_{ji}\) \[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}=\frac1p\sum_{k=1}^{p}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}. \] One example. Fix \(k\) and a weight \(w_{ji}\). The weight influences \(E_k\) only through the potential \(\xi_j\) and thus through the output \(y_j\) of neuron \(j\). By the chain rule \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}=\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}\cdot\frac{\partial y_j}{\partial w_{ji}}=\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}\cdot\frac{\partial y_j}{\partial \xi_j}\cdot\frac{\partial \xi_j}{\partial w_{ji}}=\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}\cdot\sigma_j'(\xi_j)\cdot y_i, \] since
• \(\dfrac{\partial y_j}{\partial\xi_j}=\dfrac{\partial\sigma_j(\xi_j)}{\partial\xi_j}=\sigma_j'(\xi_j)\),
• \(\dfrac{\partial\xi_j}{\partial w_{ji}}=\dfrac{\partial\sum_{r\in j_{\leftarrow}}w_{jr}y_r}{\partial w_{ji}}=y_i\) (only the term with \(r=i\) depends on \(w_{ji}\); for the bias \(i=0\) and \(y_0=1\)).

The remaining unknown factor \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j\) is computed by backpropagation (next question).
keyPoints: Chain rule: \(\partial E_k/\partial w_{ji}=\partial E_k/\partial y_j\cdot\sigma_j'(\xi_j)\cdot y_i\)
\(\partial E_k/\partial y_j\) = derivative of \(E_k\) as a function of the outputs of the layer of \(j\)
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 87–88

name: Derive the backpropagation formulas for \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j\): first for an output neuron \(j\in Y\) (squared error), then for a hidden neuron. What do the formulas become when all activations are logistic sigmoids?
answer:
Output neuron \(j\in Y\). With \(E_k=\frac12\sum_{r\in Y}(y_r-d_{kr})^2\): \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y_j}\,\frac12\sum_{r\in Y}(y_r-d_{kr})^2=y_j-d_{kj} \] (only the term \(r=j\) depends on \(y_j\); the \(\frac12\) cancels the 2).

Hidden neuron \(j\notin Y\). The output \(y_j\) influences \(E_k\) only through the neurons \(r\in j_{\rightarrow}\) to which \(j\) sends its output, i.e. \(E_k\) depends on \(y_j\) only through \(y_r\), \(r\in j_{\rightarrow}\). By the chain rule \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\cdot\frac{\partial y_r}{\partial y_j}=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\cdot\frac{\partial y_r}{\partial \xi_r}\cdot\frac{\partial \xi_r}{\partial y_j}=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\cdot\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\cdot w_{rj}, \] since \(\frac{\partial y_r}{\partial\xi_r}=\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\) and \(\frac{\partial\xi_r}{\partial y_j}=\frac{\partial\sum_{s\in r_{\leftarrow}}w_{rs}y_s}{\partial y_j}=w_{rj}\). \(\square\)

The derivative for a hidden neuron is thus expressed through the derivatives of the neurons in the layer above – the error is propagated backwards.

Logistic sigmoid (historical special case). If \(y_j=\sigma_j(\xi_j)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-\xi_j}}\) for all \(j\in Z\setminus X\), then \(\sigma_j'(\xi_j)=y_j(1-y_j)\), and thus
• \(\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=y_j-d_{kj}\) for \(j\in Y\),
• \(\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\,y_r(1-y_r)\,w_{rj}\) for \(j\in Z\setminus(Y\cup X)\).
The derivative of the activation is then obtained directly from the neuron's output computed in the forward pass.
keyPoints: Hidden: \(E_k\) depends on \(y_j\) only through \(y_r\), \(r\in j_{\rightarrow}\) → chain rule over all successors
Result: \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\partial E_k/\partial y_r\cdot\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\cdot w_{rj}\)
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 88–90

name: Describe the complete algorithm that computes the gradient \(\partial E/\partial w_{ji}\) of an MLP (forward pass, backward pass, accumulation), including the order in which backpropagation evaluates neurons and why this order works.
answer:
Goal: compute \(\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}=\dfrac1p\sum_{k=1}^{p}\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}\) for all weights.

Algorithm:
Initialize \(E_{ji}:=0\) for all weights (by the end of the computation \(E_{ji}=\partial E/\partial w_{ji}\)).
For every \(k=1,\dots,p\) do:
1. forward pass: compute \(y_j=y_j(w,x_k)\) (and \(\xi_j\)) for all \(j\in Z\);
2. backward pass: compute \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j\) for all \(j\in Z\) using backpropagation (below);
3. compute \(\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}:=\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}\cdot\sigma_j'(\xi_j)\cdot y_i\) for all weights \(w_{ji}\);
4. \(E_{ji}:=E_{ji}+\dfrac1p\cdot\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}\).
The resulting \(E_{ji}\) equals \(\partial E/\partial w_{ji}\). Steps 2 and 3 need \(\xi_j\) and \(y_j\) of all neurons, so the forward pass must store them.

Backpropagation – compute \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j\) for all \(j\in Z\):
• if \(j\in Y\), then \(\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=y_j-d_{kj}\);
• if \(j\in Z\setminus Y\), \(j\) in the \(\ell\)-th layer, and \(\partial E_k/\partial y_r\) has already been computed for all neurons in the \((\ell+1)\)-st layer, compute \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\,\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\,w_{rj}. \] Why the order works: all neurons \(r\in j_{\rightarrow}\) belong to the \((\ell+1)\)-st layer, so proceeding from the output layer downwards, layer by layer, every value needed on the right-hand side is already available. The forward pass must come first because the backward pass uses \(y_j\) and \(\xi_j\) computed in it. (Input neurons can be skipped in training: they have no incoming weights.)
keyPoints: Initialize accumulators \(E_{ji}:=0\); loop over all training examples \(k\)
Forward pass: compute and store all \(\xi_j,y_j\) for input \(x_k\)
Backward pass: \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j\) from the output layer downwards
\(\partial E_k/\partial w_{ji}:=\partial E_k/\partial y_j\cdot\sigma_j'(\xi_j)\cdot y_i\), then \(E_{ji}\mathrel{+}=\frac1p\,\partial E_k/\partial w_{ji}\)
Works because all \(r\in j_{\rightarrow}\) lie in the next layer, already processed
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 91–92

name: What is the time complexity of one gradient computation in the batch algorithm? Give the proof sketch. What can be said about the speed of convergence of gradient descent?
answer:
Claim. The computation of \(\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ji}}(w^{(t)})\) stops in time linear in the size of the network times the size of the training set (assuming unit cost of operations, including the computation of \(\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\) for a given \(\xi_r\)).

Proof sketch. The algorithm does the following \(p\) times:
1. forward pass, i.e. computes \(y_j(w,x_k)\);
2. backpropagation, i.e. computes \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j\);
3. computes \(\partial E_k/\partial w_{ji}\) and adds it to \(E_{ji}\) (a constant-time operation per weight in the unit cost framework).
Steps 1–3 take time linear in the number of network weights \(\lvert W\rvert\): in the forward pass every weight is used once (in the sum \(\xi_j=\sum_i w_{ji}y_i\)), in the backward pass every weight \(w_{rj}\) appears once in the sums over \(r\in j_{\rightarrow}\), and step 3 does constant work per weight. Repeating this for \(p\) examples gives time \(O(\lvert W\rvert\cdot p)\).

Convergence. This bounds only the cost of one gradient computation (one step). The speed of convergence of gradient descent – how many steps are needed – cannot be estimated in general.
keyPoints: Time linear in (size of the network) \(\times\) (size of the training set): \(O(\lvert W\rvert\cdot p)\)
Per example: forward pass, backpropagation, per-weight update of E_ji – each linear in the number of weights
The number of gradient-descent steps (speed of convergence) cannot be estimated in general
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 93 (per-weight counting elaborates the proof sketch)

name: Describe the online algorithm and stochastic (minibatch) gradient descent for an MLP, and compare them with the batch algorithm. State how the training example or minibatch is chosen and what an epoch is.
answer:
Online algorithm. It computes a sequence of weight vectors \(w^{(0)},w^{(1)},\dots\); the weights in \(w^{(0)}\) are randomly initialized to values close to 0; in step \(t+1\): \[ w_{ji}^{(t+1)}=w_{ji}^{(t)}+\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)},\qquad\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}=-\varepsilon(t)\cdot\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr), \] with learning rate \(0\lt\varepsilon(t)\le1\). The update uses the error \(E_k\) of a single training example \(k\in\{1,\dots,p\}\) instead of the whole \(E\); the example is taken cyclically or randomly in each step.

SGD (stochastic gradient descent with minibatches).
• the weights in \(w^{(0)}\) are randomly initialized to values close to 0;
• in step \(t+1\) (\(t=0,1,2,\dots\)): choose (randomly) a minibatch \(T\subseteq\{1,\dots,p\}\) and compute \(w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}+\Delta w^{(t)}\), where \[ \Delta w^{(t)}=-\varepsilon(t)\cdot\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\sum_{k\in T}\nabla E_k\bigl(w^{(t)}\bigr), \] \(0\lt\varepsilon(t)\le1\) is the learning rate and \(\nabla E_k(w^{(t)})\) is the gradient of the error of example \(k\).
The random choice of minibatches is typically implemented by randomly shuffling all data and then choosing minibatches sequentially. One round through all data is called an epoch.

Comparison. Batch gradient descent uses \(T=\{1,\dots,p\}\) (the exact gradient of \(E\), but every step costs a pass over the whole training set); the online algorithm is the case \(\lvert T\rvert=1\) (cheapest step, noisiest gradient); SGD with minibatches lies in between – each step is cheap and uses only an estimate of the gradient. The average \(\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\sum_{k\in T}\) is the same normalisation as the \(\frac1p\) in \(E\), so the learning rate keeps its meaning when the minibatch size changes.
keyPoints: Online: \(\Delta w_{ji}^{(t)}=-\varepsilon(t)\,\partial E_k/\partial w_{ji}\) – one training example per step (cyclic or random)
\(\Delta w^{(t)}=-\varepsilon(t)\frac1{\lvert T\rvert}\sum_{k\in T}\nabla E_k(w^{(t)})\) – average over the minibatch
Implemented by shuffling the data and taking minibatches sequentially; one round = epoch
Batch = all examples per step; minibatch gradient is only an estimate
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 95–96

name: Which output activation and error function are typically used for regression and for multi-class classification? Give the formulas.
answer:
In both cases the error is the average \(E(w)=\frac1p\sum_{k=1}^{p}E_k(w)\) over the training set \(\{(x_k,d_k)\mid k=1,\dots,p\}\), \(x_k\in\mathbb R^{\lvert X\rvert}\).

Regression.
• Output activation: typically the identity, \(y_i=\sigma(\xi_i)=\xi_i\) for \(i\in Y\).
• Desired outputs \(d_k=(d_{ki})_{i\in Y}\in\mathbb R^{\lvert Y\rvert}\).
• Error function: mean squared error (mse) \[ E_k(w)=\frac12\sum_{i\in Y}\bigl(y_i(w,x_k)-d_{ki}\bigr)^2. \] Classification.
• Output activation: softmax; with \(Y=\{j_1,\dots,j_m\}\) and \(i\in Y\) \[ y_i=\sigma_i(\xi_{j_1},\dots,\xi_{j_m})=\frac{e^{\xi_i}}{\sum_{j\in Y}e^{\xi_j}}. \] Unlike ordinary activations, softmax depends on the potentials of all output neurons; the outputs are positive and sum to 1, so they can be read as a probability distribution over the classes (a standard remark).
• Desired outputs \(d_k\in\{0,1\}^{\lvert Y\rvert}\) with exactly one component equal to 1 (\(\sum_{i\in Y}d_{ki}=1\)): the desired class is marked by 1.
• Error function: (categorical) cross-entropy \[ E_k(w)=-\sum_{i\in Y}d_{ki}\log y_i(w,x_k). \]
keyPoints: Regression: identity output activation; mse \(E_k=\frac12\sum_{i\in Y}(y_i-d_{ki})^2\)
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 97–98 (the probability reading of softmax is a standard remark, not printed on the slide)

name: Practical (derivation): For softmax outputs with one-hot desired outputs and the cross-entropy error, show that \(\partial E_k/\partial\xi_i=y_i-d_{ki}\), and then compute \(\partial E_k/\partial w_{i\ell}\) and \(\partial E_k/\partial y_\ell\) for neurons \(\ell\) of the layer \(V\) just below the output layer \(Y\).
answer:
Setting. Fix \(k\) and write \(y_i=y_i(w,x_k)\). Since \(\sum_{i\in Y}d_{ki}=1\), \[ E_k=-\sum_{i\in Y}d_{ki}\log\frac{e^{\xi_i}}{\sum_{j\in Y}e^{\xi_j}}=-\sum_{i\in Y}d_{ki}\xi_i+\sum_{i\in Y}d_{ki}\log\sum_{j\in Y}e^{\xi_j}=-\sum_{i\in Y}d_{ki}\xi_i+\log\sum_{j\in Y}e^{\xi_j}. \] Derivative w.r.t. the potential. For \(i\in Y\) \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial\xi_i}=-d_{ki}+\frac{e^{\xi_i}}{\sum_{j\in Y}e^{\xi_j}}=y_i-d_{ki}. \] Weights and previous layer. Let \(V\) be the layer just below \(Y\), so \(\xi_i=\sum_{\ell\in i_{\leftarrow}}w_{i\ell}y_\ell\). Then for \(i\in Y\), \(\ell\in i_{\leftarrow}\) \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{i\ell}}=\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial\xi_i}\cdot\frac{\partial\xi_i}{\partial w_{i\ell}}=(y_i-d_{ki})\,y_\ell, \] and for \(\ell\in V\) the output \(y_\ell\) influences \(E_k\) through all potentials \(\xi_i\), \(i\in Y\), with \(\partial\xi_i/\partial y_\ell=w_{i\ell}\): \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_\ell}=\sum_{i\in Y}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial\xi_i}\,w_{i\ell}=\sum_{i\in Y}(y_i-d_{ki})\,w_{i\ell}. \] (Equivalently, \(-\sum_i d_{ki}\bigl(w_{i\ell}-\sum_{j\in Y}y_jw_{j\ell}\bigr)\), which equals the same expression because \(\sum_id_{ki}=1\).)

Interpretation. Softmax has no separate \(\sigma_i'(\xi_i)\) factor: for \(i\in Y\) the product \(\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_i}\sigma_i'(\xi_i)\) of the general formulas is replaced by \(\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial\xi_i}=y_i-d_{ki}\), the same simple difference as for squared error with identity output. Below \(V\), backpropagation proceeds as before.
keyPoints: No \(\sigma_i'(\xi_i)\) factor: \(\partial E_k/\partial\xi_i\) replaces \(\partial E_k/\partial y_i\cdot\sigma_i'\)
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 99 (the derivation is on the slide; the equivalent form with the log-sum-exp term is derived)

name: Describe the output activation and error function used for binary classification, and explain – by computing the gradient for a single neuron with a logistic output – why cross-entropy is preferable to the squared error.
answer:
Binary classification. Assume a single output neuron \(o\), \(Y=\{o\}\).
• Output activation: logistic sigmoid \(\sigma_o(\xi_o)=\dfrac{e^{\xi_o}}{e^{\xi_o}+1}=\dfrac1{1+e^{-\xi_o}}\).
• Training dataset \(T=\{(x_1,d_1),\dots,(x_p,d_p)\}\), where \(x_k\in\mathbb R^{\lvert X\rvert}\) is the \(k\)-th input and \(d_k\in\{0,1\}\) is the desired output.
• Error function: (binary) cross-entropy, \(E=\frac1p\sum_kE_k\) with (writing \(y_o=y_o(w,x_k)\)) \[ E_k(w)=-\bigl[d_k\log y_o+(1-d_k)\log(1-y_o)\bigr]. \] Squared error vs. cross-entropy. Consider a single-neuron model \(y=\sigma(wx)=\dfrac1{1+e^{-wx}}\) with one weight \(w\in\mathbb R\) (no bias) and a training set \(T=\{(x,d)\}\), \(x\in\mathbb R\), \(d\in\{0,1\}\). Recall \(\sigma'=y(1-y)\), so \(\partial y/\partial w=y(1-y)x\).

Squared error \(E(w)=\frac12(y-d)^2\): \[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w}=(y-d)\,y\,(1-y)\,x. \] • If \(d=1\) and \(y\approx0\), then \(\partial E/\partial w\approx0\) (factor \(y\approx0\)).
• If \(d=0\) and \(y\approx1\), then \(\partial E/\partial w\approx0\) (factor \(1-y\approx0\)).
The gradient is small even though the model is wrong – the saturated sigmoid kills the gradient and learning stalls.

Cross-entropy \(E(w)=-d\log y-(1-d)\log(1-y)\):
• for \(d=1\): \(\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w}=-\dfrac1y\cdot y(1-y)x=-(1-y)\,x\), close to \(-x\) for \(y\approx0\);
• for \(d=0\): \(\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w}=\dfrac1{1-y}\cdot y(1-y)x=y\,x\), close to \(x\) for \(y\approx1\).
In both cases \(\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w}=(y-d)\,x\) (compare with softmax). The factor \(y(1-y)\) of the sigmoid derivative cancels, so the gradient is large exactly when the model is confidently wrong and the error is corrected quickly.
keyPoints: Squared error: \(\partial E/\partial w=(y-d)\,y(1-y)\,x\approx0\) when the output is saturated and wrong
The sigmoid derivative cancels → large gradient when the model is wrong
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf (2026 deck), printed slides 100–101 (the d=0 case written as 1/(1-y)·y(1-y)x = yx; the slide writes the equivalent product with two minus signs)

name: Define a computational graph and its semantics (how it is evaluated). Show how an \(L\)-layer MLP is expressed as a computational graph.
answer:
Computational graph. Consider a directed acyclic graph \((U,A)\) with node set \(U\) and arc set \(A\). Individual nodes are denoted by \(u,v\). For a node \(u\), denote by \(u_{\leftarrow}\) the set of all nodes \(v\) with \((v,u)\in A\) and by \(u_{\rightarrow}\) the set of all nodes \(v\) with \((u,v)\in A\).
• input nodes are nodes with \(u_{\leftarrow}=\emptyset\);
• output nodes are nodes with \(u_{\rightarrow}=\emptyset\);
• hidden nodes are the remaining nodes.
Each node \(u\) has its output value \(y^{(u)}\) (in general a vector). Each non-input node \(u\) is assigned a function \(f^{(u)}\) such that \[ y^{(u)}=f^{(u)}\bigl(y^{(u_1)},\dots,y^{(u_q)}\bigr),\qquad u_{\leftarrow}=\{u_1,\dots,u_q\} \] (assuming a fixed ordering on \(u_{\leftarrow}\)).

Semantics.
Input: a collection of vectors \(v^{(u)}\), one for each input node \(u\).
Computation: start with \(y^{(u)}=v^{(u)}\) for every input node \(u\); while there are nodes that have not been evaluated, select a node \(u\) all of whose predecessors have been evaluated and compute \(y^{(u)}=f^{(u)}(y^{(u_1)},\dots,y^{(u_q)})\).
Output: the collection of values of all output nodes.
Because the graph is acyclic, such a node always exists until all nodes are evaluated.

\(L\)-layer MLP as a graph. Take the chain graph with \(U=\{0,1,\dots,L\}\) and \(A=\{(\ell-1,\ell)\mid\ell=1,\dots,L\}\). Each node \(\ell=1,\dots,L\) is a whole layer and is assigned \[ y^{(\ell)}=f^{(\ell)}\bigl(y^{(\ell-1)}\bigr)=\sigma^{(\ell)}\bigl(W^{(\ell)}y^{(\ell-1)}\bigr), \] where \(W^{(\ell)}\) is a weight matrix and \(\sigma^{(\ell)}=(\sigma^{(\ell)}_1,\dots,\sigma^{(\ell)}_r)\) is a vector of activation functions applied component-wise: \(\sigma^{(\ell)}(z_1,\dots,z_r)=(\sigma^{(\ell)}_1(z_1),\dots,\sigma^{(\ell)}_r(z_r))\). The input node 0 gets a vector as input and the output node \(L\) gives a vector as output. (Biases can be included by appending a constant component 1 to \(y^{(\ell-1)}\); this remark is derived.)
keyPoints: Input nodes: \(u_{\leftarrow}=\emptyset\); output nodes: \(u_{\rightarrow}=\emptyset\); others hidden
Each non-input node has a function: \(y^{(u)}=f^{(u)}(y^{(u_1)},\dots,y^{(u_q)})\)
Evaluate any node whose predecessors are all evaluated, until done
source: PV021 L3 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 104–106 (not in the 2026 deck)

name: How is differentiation defined between two connected nodes of a computational graph? Define the Jacobian matrix \(\partial y^{(u)}/\partial y^{(v)}\) and compute it for the layers of the MLP graph.
answer:
We are interested in the rate of change of \(y^{(u)}\) with changes in \(y^{(v)}\).

Jacobian. Given two nodes \(u,v\) with \((v,u)\in A\), where \(y^{(u)}\) has \(I\) components and \(y^{(v)}\) has \(J\) components, \(\dfrac{\partial y^{(u)}}{\partial y^{(v)}}\) denotes the \(I\times J\) Jacobian matrix \[ \frac{\partial y^{(u)}}{\partial y^{(v)}}=\left(\frac{\partial y^{(u)}_i}{\partial y^{(v)}_j}\right)_{i=1..I,\;j=1..J}, \qquad \frac{\partial y^{(u)}_i}{\partial y^{(v)}_j}=\frac{\partial\bigl(f^{(u)}(y^{(u_1)},\dots,y^{(u_q)})\bigr)_i}{\partial y^{(v)}_j}. \] Rows correspond to components of the output of node \(u\), columns to components of the output of node \(v\).

MLP example. In the \(L\)-layer MLP graph with \(y^{(\ell)}=\sigma^{(\ell)}(W^{(\ell)}y^{(\ell-1)})\) put \(\xi^{(\ell)}=W^{(\ell)}y^{(\ell-1)}\). The Jacobian is \[ \frac{\partial y^{(\ell)}}{\partial y^{(\ell-1)}}=\dot\sigma^{(\ell)}\,W^{(\ell)},\qquad \dot\sigma^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{diag}\bigl(\sigma^{(\ell)\prime}_1(\xi^{(\ell)}_1),\dots,\sigma^{(\ell)\prime}_r(\xi^{(\ell)}_r)\bigr), \] the diagonal matrix of derivatives of the components of \(\sigma^{(\ell)}\) evaluated at the inner potentials \(\xi^{(\ell)}\) of the layer.

Check with components: \(y^{(\ell)}_i=\sigma^{(\ell)}_i\bigl(\sum_jW^{(\ell)}_{ij}y^{(\ell-1)}_j\bigr)\), so \(\dfrac{\partial y^{(\ell)}_i}{\partial y^{(\ell-1)}_j}=\sigma^{(\ell)\prime}_i(\xi^{(\ell)}_i)\,W^{(\ell)}_{ij}\), exactly the \((i,j)\) entry of \(\dot\sigma^{(\ell)}W^{(\ell)}\) – the same quantity \(\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\,w_{rj}\) that appears in the neuron-level backpropagation formula.
keyPoints: \(\partial y^{(u)}/\partial y^{(v)}\) is the Jacobian: entry \((i,j)=\partial y^{(u)}_i/\partial y^{(v)}_j\)
Defined for nodes with \((v,u)\in A\); \(I\times J\) matrix

name: Formulate backpropagation for general computational graphs, and apply it to the MLP graph extended by an error node to obtain the layer-wise backward recursion.
answer:
General backpropagation. Fix a node \(o\). Our aim is to compute \(\dfrac{\partial y^{(o)}}{\partial y^{(u)}}\) for all predecessors \(u\) of \(o\) in the computational graph.
• Base: \(\dfrac{\partial y^{(o)}}{\partial y^{(o)}}=I\), the identity matrix.
• Recursion: by the (appropriately general version of the) chain rule \[ \frac{\partial y^{(o)}}{\partial y^{(u)}}=\sum_{v\in u_{\rightarrow}}\frac{\partial y^{(o)}}{\partial y^{(v)}}\cdot\frac{\partial y^{(v)}}{\partial y^{(u)}}, \] a sum over all successors \(v\) of \(u\) of products of Jacobian matrices.
• A node can be processed once \(\partial y^{(o)}/\partial y^{(v)}\) is known for all its successors \(v\), i.e. nodes are processed in the reverse of the evaluation order. The local Jacobians are evaluated at the values computed in the forward evaluation of the graph.

MLP with an error node. Consider the MLP graph with one additional "error" node: \(U=\{0,1,\dots,L,o\}\), \(A=\{(\ell-1,\ell)\mid\ell=1,\dots,L\}\cup\{(L,o)\}\); each node \(\ell=1,\dots,L\) is assigned \(y^{(\ell)}=\sigma^{(\ell)}(W^{(\ell)}y^{(\ell-1)})\), and \(f^{(o)}\) is the error function (e.g. the squared error) applied to the network output \(y^{(L)}\).

Backprop:
• \(\partial y^{(o)}/\partial y^{(L)}\) is the derivative of the error function (for the squared error \(\frac12\lVert y^{(L)}-d\rVert^2\) it is the row vector \((y^{(L)}-d)^{T}\));
• for \(\ell\le L\) the node \(\ell-1\) has the single successor \(\ell\), so \[ \frac{\partial y^{(o)}}{\partial y^{(\ell-1)}}=\frac{\partial y^{(o)}}{\partial y^{(\ell)}}\cdot\frac{\partial y^{(\ell)}}{\partial y^{(\ell-1)}}=\frac{\partial y^{(o)}}{\partial y^{(\ell)}}\cdot\dot\sigma^{(\ell)}W^{(\ell)}. \] Starting at the top and multiplying by \(\dot\sigma^{(\ell)}W^{(\ell)}\) layer by layer gives the derivative of the error w.r.t. the outputs of every layer – the matrix form of the neuron-level rule \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\partial E_k/\partial y_r\cdot\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\cdot w_{rj}\).
keyPoints: Fix node \(o\); compute \(\partial y^{(o)}/\partial y^{(u)}\) for all predecessors \(u\)
Chain rule: \(\partial y^{(o)}/\partial y^{(u)}=\sum_{v\in u_{\rightarrow}}(\partial y^{(o)}/\partial y^{(v)})(\partial y^{(v)}/\partial y^{(u)})\)
MLP graph plus error node \(o\) with arc \((L,o)\); \(f^{(o)}\) = error function
\(\partial y^{(o)}/\partial y^{(\ell-1)}=(\partial y^{(o)}/\partial y^{(\ell)})\,\dot\sigma^{(\ell)}W^{(\ell)}\), starting from the derivative of the error
